titre: The first two Dogme films broke their own authors' vow
accroche: Dogme 95 imposes ten rules on itself in 1995, including one against crediting the director. Three years later, its first two films already break them.
contenu_vulgarise:
A set with no outside props, a handheld camera, and credits in which the director must not appear: that is what ten rules announced in 1995 by two Danish filmmakers require. The movement's first two films, released in 1998, each already carry a violation.

## Ten rules written in forty-five minutes

On March 13, 1995, in Paris, at the conference “Cinema Toward Its Second Century,” Lars von Trier throws red leaflets into the audience: he announces Dogme 95, which he founded with Thomas Vinterberg. The two men sign the text, and Vinterberg has said they wrote it in forty-five minutes. It comes down to ten points, the “Vow of Chastity”: shoot on location, with no props or sets brought in; never produce sound separately from the image, music being allowed only if it exists where the scene is shot; film handheld; in color, with no special lighting; with no optical work or filters; with no superficial action, which rules out murders and weapons; with no distancing in time or space, the action taking place here and now; with no genre films; in Academy 35 mm format; and the director must not be credited.

Kristian Levring and Søren Kragh-Jacobsen then join von Trier and Vinterberg, and the group calls itself the Dogme 95 Collective, or the Dogme Brethren. The movement's film number one is *Festen* (Vinterberg, 1998), number two *Idioterne* (von Trier, 1998).

## What this shifts

A vow is a commitment you take upon yourself, and those who wrote it did not keep it to the letter. According to Wikipedia, Vinterberg “confessed” to having covered a window during a scene of *Festen*, and von Trier used Saint-Saëns's *Le Cygne* (*The Swan*) as background sound in *Idioterne*. The first two certified films thus each carry a violation of their own authors' rules.

*Breaking the Waves* (1996), von Trier's first film after the movement's founding, shows the gap in the other direction. Wikipedia describes it as heavily influenced by the style and spirit of Dogme 95, yet it breaks many rules, including constructed sets, post-synchronized music and computer-generated images at the end of the film. It isn't counted among the movement's films, which begins with *Festen*.

The Vow of Chastity thus serves as a horizon more than as a rulebook applied to the letter: the movement made constraint its principle, and its first two films already bear the mark of a violation.

repere.texte: A year after announcing the Vow of Chastity with Thomas Vinterberg, Lars von Trier makes Breaking the Waves (1996), heavily influenced by the style and spirit of Dogme 95 but breaking many rules: constructed sets, post-synchronized music, computer-generated images at the end of the film.

carte.punch: The first two Dogme films broke the vow of their own authors.
carte.idee: In 1995, von Trier and Vinterberg announce Dogme 95 and its ten rules. In 1998, Festen (a covered window) and Idioterne (background music) are released, each with a violation, according to Wikipedia.

quiz.question: What does the tenth and last rule of the Dogme 95 Vow of Chastity stipulate?
choix: The director must appear on screen, in a brief scene of the film
The director must not be credited
The film must be shot in a single take, with no later editing
The screenplay must be written jointly by at least two authors
quiz.explication: The English and Danish versions of Wikipedia give the same tenth rule: the director must not be credited. None of the ten rules requires an appearance by the director, a single shot with no editing or joint writing, and the ninth merely requires the Academy 35 mm format.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where and when does Lars von Trier publicly announce the Dogme 95 movement?
choix: On March 13, 1995, in Paris, for cinema's hundredth anniversary
On March 13, 1995, in Copenhagen, at a local film festival
In 1998, at Cannes, at the presentation of the first certified film
In 1996, in Berlin, at the international film festival
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The movement is announced on March 13, 1995, in Paris, at a conference organized for cinema's hundredth anniversary, where von Trier hands out leaflets presenting Dogme 95.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What are the first two films certified by Dogme 95, and in what year are they released?
choix: Breaking the Waves and Dancer in the Dark, in 1996
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wikipedia numbers Festen (Vinterberg) Dogme #1 and Idioterne (von Trier) Dogme #2, both from 1998; Mifune is number 3 and Lovers (1999) number 5.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the relationship between Breaking the Waves (1996) and Dogme 95?
choix: It is the movement's first certified film, released before Festen
It was made before the movement was announced, in 1993
It is a Vinterberg film, shot in compliance with the ten rules
Von Trier's first film after the founding, influenced by the spirit of the movement but breaking many rules
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wikipedia describes Breaking the Waves as von Trier's first film after the founding of Dogme 95, heavily influenced by its style and spirit, but breaking many rules (constructed sets, post-synchronized music, computer-generated images). The movement's first film is Festen, in 1998.
